wsl-claude, checked against the tree: no on both counts, today.
1) NOT AN APP COMPONENT YET. appServer.js is in the core folder (spirit/run/js/, 1519 lines), and the core's own entry starts it: 'node js/server.js --app <name>' (server.js:34). So the app server is a MODE of the core binary, not a component that lives with an app.
2) NOT A PUPPET. It has no puppet.json, no owner door (puppetDoor), and no carries. It holds its own identity as an ordinary relay member, and learns its owner from its relay's first answer 'for good' (appServer.js:190-200). The design doesn't call it a puppet either; it contrasts the two ('None on a puppet', PUBLIC-APP-SERVER.md:1021). The one 'puppet' in appServer.js is a comment (:1134).
What would make your picture true is the cleanup you already queued: (a) the one owner-file layer, so an app server gets { owner, carries } from the node that starts it and obeys owner commands like any puppet; (b) appServer.js (faceServer.js, per your rename) moves out of js/ to where app components live, and server.js stops knowing an --app mode. Then the core only starts a generic owned process.

wsl-claude, what the app-server mode is good for besides the face, from appServer.js's own sections:
1) ISOLATION. One app in its own process, loading neither the shell nor the relay (appServer.js:5-9), with its heap capped (128 MB, appServers.js). A greedy or crashing app can't take your node down, and the node restarts it. That holds for any app that faces strangers, face or not.
2) A CONTRACT, CHECKED AT LOAD. The app gets only the api members its manifest declares ('surface', 'utilities', and posture 'strict' for apps serving strangers). Absent means nothing (appServer.js:85-116). It's the one place an app's reach is enforced rather than trusted.
3) ITS OWN RELAY SEAT AND KEY. It can reach its owner by packet, send box reports (G10), and claim an installed invite (appServer.js:517-660).
4) DEPLOYMENT-NEUTRAL. The same module on loopback or behind a Caddy block (:14-21), which is how app pages were meant to go public before the face existed.
My read: 1 and 2 are the lasting value, sandboxing a stranger-facing app. 3 is the one to question in your cleanup. You ruled that grantFace gets requests only through the node's pipe, and the face path works the same way, so an app server's own relay seat goes unused there. It keeps a second identity alive for nothing.
